sections.h2: What is the South Carolina homestead exemption?
sections.html:
It exempts the first $50,000 of the fair market value of a dwelling place from county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes for owners who are 65 or older, totally and permanently disabled, or legally blind. The rule is in S.C. Code 12-37-250.

It is a tax exemption on the home, not a creditor protection and not a freeze on the value. The South Carolina Department of Revenue describes it as a complete exemption from taxes on the first $50,000 of fair market value of your legal residence, and it is handled through the county auditor. You can read the statute on the Legislature's Chapter 37 page and the agency summary on the SCDOR exemptions page.

An owner qualifies by age, disability or blindness, and by holding the right kind of title to the dwelling.

  • Age: a South Carolina resident for at least one year who turned 65 on or before December 31.
  • Disability: someone classified as totally and permanently disabled by a state or federal agency. A person who is not classified can ask the state Vocational Rehabilitation agency to evaluate the claim.
  • Blindness: a person who is legally blind as defined in Section 43-25-20.
  • Title: the owner needs complete fee simple title or a life estate. Life estates created by will count.

A home owned jointly by spouses qualifies when either spouse meets the test before January 1 of the tax year and the one-year residency requirement is met. The statute defines permanent and total disability as the inability to do substantial gainful work because of a medically determinable impairment lasting, or expected to last, at least 12 continuous months or ending in death.

sections.h2: How do you apply, and by when?
sections.html:
Apply in writing to the county auditor before July 16 of the tax year. An application filed after July 15 normally applies to the next year, with one exception for filings made before the first penalty date.

The statute allows three routes: in person at the auditor's office, by mail with proof of age, disability or blindness, or online where the auditor can check official records. Failing to apply waives the exemption for that year. The SCDOR says the individual form is PT-401I and that processing is currently 10 to 12 weeks, with MyDORWAY as the fastest filing method.

The SCDOR page also notes that for tax year 2026 the state temporarily authorized an additional amount for certain recipients, and the county auditor decides whether it applies to you.

sections.h2: How is the homestead exemption different from the 4 percent legal residence rate?
sections.html:
They are two separate breaks. The 4 percent legal residence assessment lowers the taxable share of value for an owner-occupied home, while the homestead exemption removes the first $50,000 of value for qualifying seniors, disabled owners and blind owners.

The SCDOR states that the legal residence must be approved before a real estate exemption is granted, and the legal residence application goes through the county assessor. Under 12-43-220(c), the 4 percent ratio covers the home and up to five contiguous acres that the owner occupies as a legal residence. Other real property is assessed at 6 percent.

  • The legal residence application must be made before the first penalty date for the first tax year the owner claims it.
  • A residence rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year loses the 4 percent rate.
  • An owner who is found ineligible, or who fails to tell the assessor within six months of losing eligibility, can owe a penalty of 100 percent of the tax plus interest at one-half of one percent per month.

sections.h2: What happens to the exemption when you sell the house?
sections.html:
The exemption belongs to the owner's permanent home, so it stops with the sale and a buyer does not inherit it. The statute defines the dwelling place as the applicant's permanent home and legal residence.

A seller who moves in South Carolina can claim the exemption on the new residence, and a surviving spouse who moves must tell the auditor of the new address. A surviving spouse can also keep the exemption on the current home if they take complete fee simple title or a life estate within nine months of the death, and it continues while the spouse stays unmarried and uses it as a permanent home (12-37-250(D)).

The statute also says the exemption does not trigger a reassessment of the property. The five-year reappraisal cycle in 12-43-217 still runs on its own schedule, and a county may postpone implementing new values by one tax year.

sections.h2: How do taxes get handled at closing in South Carolina?
sections.html:
Real estate taxes are billed a year behind and are due between September 30 and January 15, so the closing statement usually splits the year between buyer and seller. The statute puts the penalty at 3 percent after January 15, with 7 percent more after February 2 and another 5 percent after March 17 (12-45-70 and 12-45-180).

If title changes after assessment, a new owner can ask the auditor to apportion the taxes and costs owed by the original owner before any tax-execution sale (12-45-140). When title transfers during the year and the notice went to the prior owner, the treasurer must waive penalties if the current owner never got a timely notice (12-45-180(B)).

The deed also carries a recording fee of $1.85 per $500 of value, made up of $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county (12-24-10). The grantor generally owes it (12-24-20). Confirm the numbers with your closing attorney and county office.

sections.h2: Can owners with other situations get relief?
sections.html:
Yes, several other exemptions exist, each with its own rules and form.

  • Disabled veterans: a dwelling with a lot not exceeding five acres.
  • Paraplegic or hemiplegic persons: a dwelling and lot up to one acre.
  • Medal of Honor or former prisoner of war recipients: a dwelling and lot up to one acre.
  • Disabled law enforcement officers and firefighters with service-connected disability: a dwelling with a lot not exceeding five acres.

These come from 12-37-220(B) and the SCDOR page. Ask your county auditor which fits before you list a home, since the right exemption can lower the carrying cost while you are waiting to sell.

sections.h2: Does the exemption cover mobile homes or shared ownership?
sections.html:
Yes in some cases. An owner of a mobile home on leased land may receive the exemption against personal property taxes under the same procedures, but cannot receive both the real and the personal property exemption in the same year (12-37-250(B)).

An owner-lessee who will own the home when the lease ends qualifies as though holding fee simple or a life estate. A part owner gets the owned percentage of the full exemption, with ownership under 5 percent treated as 5 percent, and the exemption cannot exceed the value of that interest (12-37-250(J)). Heirs who inherit a share of a parent's home should keep this in mind before a sale.

faqs.q: How much is the South Carolina homestead exemption?
faqs.a: The first $50,000 of the fair market value of your dwelling place is exempt from county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes, under S.C. Code 12-37-250(A)(1).

faqs.q: What age do you have to be?
faqs.a: You must be 65 by December 31 and have lived in South Carolina for at least one year. Totally and permanently disabled and legally blind owners qualify without the age test.
Written applications must be made before July 16 of the tax year. A later application generally takes effect the following year.

faqs.q: Does a buyer keep my homestead exemption?
faqs.a: No. The exemption applies to the applicant's permanent home and legal residence, so a buyer must qualify on their own and apply to the county auditor.

faqs.q: Does the exemption apply to a rental?
faqs.a: The 4 percent legal residence rate is lost if the home is rented more than 72 days in a calendar year, and the homestead exemption requires the home to be the owner's permanent residence.
